cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: test coverage sits at 31%, there is no coverage gate in continuous integration, and production systems of comparable complexity typically run 40-60% coverage.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in continuous integration. This falls below the 40 to 60% typical for production systems of comparable complexity, meaning a regression can reach production unchallenged.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: deployments are performed manually by one engineer via SSH, there is no rollback procedure, and the last rollback attempt (8 months ago) took over 3 hours to complete.
cases.output: The most recent rollback attempt, 8 months ago, took over 3 hours to complete, and deployments are performed manually by a single engineer via SSH with no documented rollback procedure. This creates a single point of failure with no mitigation underway. A production incident requiring a rollback would depend entirely on one person's availability and manual execution, with no tested process to guide either the decision or the steps involved.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: one engineer holds sole access to the production database credentials, there is no documented access-handover process, and that engineer is on a rolling month-to-month contract.
cases.output: Production database credentials are held by a single engineer with no documented access-handover process, and that engineer operates under a rolling month-to-month contract. Departure—planned or unplanned—would immediately lock the company out of its own database. There is no compensating control. This represents a critical dependency on contract continuity and individual knowledge with no mitigation in place.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: customer personal data is retained indefinitely with no deletion policy, and there is no documented process for handling a data-subject deletion request.
cases.output: Customer personal data is retained indefinitely, with no documented deletion policy or procedure for handling data-subject deletion requests. Retention decisions rest entirely on individual discretion, and no audit trail documents what data exists or when it was collected. This gap exposes the company to regulatory liability under data-protection regimes that require deletion on request and impose statutory timelines for response. We recommend establishing a data retention schedule, implementing automated deletion for records past their business need, and documenting the process for fulfilling deletion requests within your jurisdiction's required timeframe.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) covering ALL of these facts: test coverage is 31%, there is no CI coverage gate, the last three production incidents were caused by untested edge cases, deployments are manual, and there is no rollback procedure. Do not omit any fact.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in continuous integration. The last 3 production incidents were each caused by untested edge cases that reached production unchallenged. Deployments occur manually without a documented rollback procedure, creating compounding risk: a regression can propagate to production with no automated safeguard, and reversing it requires unscripted work under pressure.

cases.input: Write three separate due-diligence findings, one paragraph each, clearly separated by a blank line. Finding 1 facts: passwords are stored in plaintext in the users table. Finding 2 facts: deployments are manual with no rollback procedure. Finding 3 facts: code comment style is inconsistent across the codebase, with no linting rule enforcing a convention.
cases.output:
Passwords are stored in plaintext within the users table, exposed to any database user and to anyone with access to backups or logs. This eliminates the primary technical barrier to account compromise across the entire user base. No hashing algorithm is applied, salting is absent, and password reuse across accounts means a single database breach exposes credentials for external systems. We strongly recommend adopting a standard key derivation function (PBKDF2, bcrypt, or Argon2) with a salt generated per user and stored alongside the hashed password.

Deployments are performed manually via SSH by individual engineers with no documented rollback procedure and no automated recovery path. The most recent rollback attempt, 8 months ago, took over 3 hours to complete. A production incident requiring reversion cannot be resolved by the team with confidence or speed, and the time required to restore service grows with each passing month as the team turns over. We recommend implementing an automated deployment pipeline with a rollback mechanism that the team has exercised at least quarterly, and documenting the procedure in a runbook reviewed by all engineers involved in release decisions.

Code comment style varies across the codebase with no enforced convention, creating friction during code review and making it harder for new engineers to follow project norms. No linting rule validates comment formatting, and style decisions have not been documented. This is typical in teams of the company's size and below, and it does not impede code clarity at the current phase. Establishing a documented style guide tied to a pre-commit linting step would reduce review cycles and accelerate onboarding. A single weekend sprint is sufficient to implement this change.
